switch_ask: Ammonia has a lone pair, and a silver ion can accept one. What can two ammonia molecules and one silver ion form?
park_text: Each silver ion is held by two ammonia molecules as Ag(NH₃)₂⁺. So little silver stays free that silver chloride keeps dissolving.

ask: Why does adding ammonia make silver chloride, an insoluble salt, dissolve? Which two equilibria are linked?

show: Here is how a chemist would put it: ammonia's lone pairs bind silver ions as Ag(NH₃)₂⁺; so little silver stays free that silver chloride keeps dissolving. Now say it in your own words.
The complex forms almost completely; to find the free silver, use its breakup: \( K_d = \dfrac{1}{K_f} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{Ag^+}][\mathrm{NH_3}]^2}{[\mathrm{Ag(NH_3)_2^+}]} \). Pick it.
After mixing (100.0 mL): Ag⁺ 0.0050 M, NH₃ 0.500 M. All the silver forms the complex: [complex] = 0.0050 M; NH₃ left = 0.500 − 2 × 0.0050 = 0.490 M. Type both.
After mixing (100.0 mL): Ag⁺ 0.0050 M, NH₃ 0.0101 M. [complex] = 0.0050 M; NH₃ left = 0.0101 − 2 × 0.0050 = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M. Type both.
x will be about 10⁻⁹, tiny next to 0.0050 and 0.490: drop it. Pick the small-x method.
With only 10⁻⁴ M ammonia left, x is not small next to it. Pick the exact method.
\( x = 5.9 \times 10^{-8} \times 0.0050 \div 0.490^2 = 1.2 \times 10^{-9} \) M. Type it with its unit.
Solving exactly, \( x = 3.8 \times 10^{-4} \) M. Type it with its unit.
\( 0.0050 \div 1.2 \times 10^{-9} = 4.1 \times 10^{6} \): four million times smaller. Type it.
